claims.text: A homogeneous distribution of reactive elements such as Al, Cr, and Ti promotes preferential formation of a continuous, adherent spinel oxide layer during elevated-temperature exposure.
The resulting spinel oxide layer retards further oxidation.
AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 can be produced by inert-gas atomization followed by spark plasma sintering.
The atomized and SPS-processed AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 alloy has a dense microstructure.
The atomized and SPS-processed alloy has a uniform microstructure with well-distributed reactive elements.
Changing SPS cooling rates can create samples with different degrees of microstructural homogeneity and reactive-element distribution.
Oxidation behavior relevant to the hypothesis occurs during isothermal exposure in air at 800–900 °C.
A continuous and adherent spinel film acts as a diffusion barrier.
The quality of the protective oxide film is governed by the microscale distribution of reactive alloying elements.
Selective oxidation of well-distributed reactive elements produces a stable, slow-growing protective spinel layer.
The spinel layer limits oxidation by reducing oxygen ingress and outward diffusion of metal ions.
More homogeneous reactive-element distributions produce thicker, more continuous, and more adherent spinel films than inhomogeneous distributions.
Samples with more homogeneous reactive-element distributions exhibit lower oxidation weight gain and reduced oxidation depth.
Less-uniform elemental distributions form discontinuous or less-adherent oxide films and therefore oxidize faster.
The hypothesis applies to multiphase HEAs processed by routes similar to inert-gas atomization and SPS.
The hypothesis is bounded to oxidative environments around 800–900 °C while bulk composition remains constant and microstructural homogeneity is varied.
Secondary phases such as sigma phase and grain-boundary effects may also affect oxidation behavior.
